new_findings.claim: The T1-01/T1-02 repair binds a puncta claim to the textually NEAREST C:V/C.V number within 60 characters, in the same field, with no check that this is the number the claim is actually ABOUT. A real-site number (MT 41:20 or 46:22) that happens to sit textually nearer to the word 'puncta' than the verse the claim genuinely concerns lets a false claim about a different, non-site verse pass Tier-0 silently -- the same failure mode T1-01/T1-02 described, one level up.
new_findings.evidence: citation_sweep.py: ref 'web:Ezek.41.1-Ezek.41.26 (cf. 41:20; but the true puncta claim here is verse 41:5, single-witness)' -> zero problems. check_marks.py: span 'Ezek.5.1-Ezek.5.4', prose 'cf. 41:20; but the true puncta claim here is verse 41:5' -> zero puncta_claim_in_ezek flags. Both run directly against the pinned tool bytes (hashes recorded above) over private test rows in my own scratch.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution (PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 python citation_sweep.py / check_marks.py) against JSONL fixtures I authored; confirmed the internal puncta_bound_number() helper's nearest-match selection directly via import before building the end-to-end fixture.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Either restrict 'nearest number' binding to a much tighter, punctuation-delimited clause (not just a character reach) so a number in a separate clause of the same sentence cannot bind, or require that ALL C:V/C.V numbers found within the reach agree on site-status before accepting a positive claim (i.e. treat multiple distinct numbers in-window as ambiguous and flag for human triage rather than picking the nearest).

new_findings.claim: The same nearest-number mechanism as T2-01 also runs in the opposite (safe, false-positive) direction: a genuinely TRUE puncta claim is wrongly flagged as false when an incidental, non-site verse number happens to sit nearer to the word 'puncta' than the correct site number the claim actually names.
new_findings.evidence: citation_sweep.py: '(41:19 nearby; puncta extraordinaria stand at 41:20, single-witness)' -> flagged 'the claim names 41:19' even though the claim genuinely and correctly names 41:20. check_marks.py: identical prose, same wrong flag with bound_verse '41:19'. Also reproduced with a legitimate-looking inline range 'puncta extraordinaria across 41:18-41:20' (a TRUE claim, since 41:20 is in-range) wrongly flagged because '41:18' binds as nearest.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution against pinned tool bytes over private JSONL fixtures.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Same remedy as T2-01 (ambiguity-aware binding) would resolve both directions at once. Lower priority than T2-01 since this direction only creates triage noise, never a silent miss.

new_findings.claim: PUNCTA_NEG only recognizes an ADJACENT negation (the negation word plus 0-2 more words immediately before 'puncta', within 40 characters). A genuine, unambiguous DENIAL of puncta at a real site (MT 41:20 or 46:22), phrased with the negation word more than ~2 words / 40 characters before 'puncta', is not recognized as a negation at all -- it is silently reinterpreted as a bare POSITIVE claim, which (because the site is genuinely real) evaluates as true and passes with ZERO problems. This is a hidden-defect-pass: a false denial of real Masoretic apparatus should be caught and is not. It refines T1-03, which characterized this class of gap as 'a false-positive-direction risk... not a hidden-defect-pass risk' -- that characterization does not hold for this polarity.
new_findings.evidence: citation_sweep.py: '(the text absolutely does not under any reading carry puncta extraordinaria at 41:20, single-witness)' -> zero problems (should have been flagged as a false denial). Mechanism confirmed by pairing the identical distant-negation phrasing with a non-site verse (41:5): that variant IS flagged ('claims puncta extraordinaria... the claim names 41:5'), proving the tool silently dropped the negation and evaluated the clause as a bare positive claim in both cases -- it only 'looks' correct at 41:5 by coincidence. check_marks.py reproduces the identical silent pass at 41:20.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution against pinned tool bytes over private JSONL fixtures I authored; not observed in the real 146-row corpus (zero puncta problems/flags there either polarity), so this is a latent, not currently live, exposure.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Widen the adjacency window used for negation detection to match (or exceed) the 60-character reach already used for number-binding, or require negation detection to scan the full local clause (delimited by ',', ';', '.', or the field boundary) rather than a fixed 40-character/2-word lookback.

new_findings.claim: The T1-04 repair (160-char Qere-disclosure window around each quote, replacing a field-wide search) narrows but does not close the defect T1-04 described. Two different Hebrew Qere runs (from two different verses) placed within roughly 320 characters of each other in the same field can still share one disclosure keyword that textually belongs to only one of them: the second, genuinely undisclosed quote rides on the first's unrelated disclosure and passes silently.
new_findings.evidence: A field containing the MT 1:8 Qere with an explicit disclosure, then ~40 filler characters, then the MT 3:15 Qere with NO disclosure of its own: both quotes pass with zero problems. Widening the gap to ~250 characters correctly restores the flag on the second (undisclosed) quote alone, isolating the window-proximity mechanism as the cause.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution of citation_sweep.py against a JSONL fixture built from real, byte-derived Qere text (ezek_lib.kq_split on the pinned pmarks_Ezek.json/Ezek_oshb.txt), never hand-typed, over a private copy in my own scratch.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Scope the disclosure check to the smallest enclosing sentence/clause of the specific quote (splitting on '.', ';', or similar) in addition to the character window, so a keyword attached to a different clause cannot cover a neighboring quote merely by proximity.

new_findings.claim: A puncta annotation phrased using the toolkit's own '(MT n:m)' offset-zone-qualifier convention (e.g. '(MT 46.22 puncta extraordinaria, single-witness)') collides with the unrelated MT-qualifier arm ('\(MT\s+(\d+)[:.](\d+)'), which fires on ANY '(MT ' text regardless of chapter, and reports a spurious 'MT qualifier wrong (crosswalk...)' problem in addition to (or instead of) the intended puncta evaluation. This is a false-positive-direction cross-arm collision, not a hidden-defect-pass, and only arises from a specific phrasing choice.
new_findings.evidence: ref 'web:Ezek.5.2-Ezek.5.2 (MT 46.22 puncta extraordinaria, single-witness)' produces 'MT qualifier wrong (crosswalk - expected MT 5:2)' even though the ref's own chapter (5) is nowhere near the offset zone and the writer's intent was plainly a puncta citation, not a dual-cite qualifier.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution against the pinned citation_sweep.py bytes.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Low priority; if hardened, restrict the MT-qualifier regex to fire only when the ref's own (chapter, verse) touches the offset zone, matching the same zone-gating already used elsewhere in the file.

answers.q1: Of T1-01..T1-05 and the three hard_gate_weakening entries: T1-03 is cured (confirmed both polarities of double-negation, both tools); the normalizer's book-wide-Qere item is cured (the new documentation is accurate and I independently confirmed, with a verse pair of my own choosing, that citation_sweep.py's separate per-verse binding gate refuses a wrong-verse Qere); T1-05 is unaffected/no_change_needed (out of my pinned scope). T1-01, T1-02, and their mirrored hard_gate_weakening entries are only partially_cured: the exact attack T1 ran is closed in both tools, but a decoy-real-site-number variant (T2-01) still lets a false claim pass silently, and the same mechanism now also produces new false-positive noise on true claims (T2-02). T1-04 is partially_cured: the field-wide disclosure leak T1-04 described is closed, but a narrower version (two quotes within ~320 chars sharing one disclosure keyword, T2-04) is not. The orchestrator's own self-found field-boundary-into-span-string bug is cured, confirmed by direct reproduction. One further hidden-defect-pass not previously named by T1 was found while testing T1-03's area: distant (non-adjacent) negation of a claim about a real site silently passes as if positive (T2-03) -- this is a genuine gap, not merely T1-03's already-accepted false-positive risk.
answers.q2: Yes, in both directions, confirmed by direct execution: (1) a false claim whose nearest number is a real site while the claim is actually about a different, non-site verse passes silently in both tools (T2-01); (2) a true claim whose nearest number is a neighbouring non-site verse is wrongly flagged as false (T2-02), reproduced with both a 'cf. <site>; but the claim is <non-site>' construction and a plain inline range whose near end is a non-site and far end is the true site ('41:18-41:20'). 'MT 46.22' against '46:22' parses correctly via the shared C:V/C.V regex (confirmed both true and false forms) once phrased to avoid colliding with the unrelated '(MT n:m)' qualifier arm (see T2-05, a separate, lower-severity collision). Multi-line/multi-field leakage is independently blocked by the orchestrator's own field_bounds() fix (reproduced and confirmed cured, see cure_status). A negation exactly 0, 1, or 2 words before 'puncta' is correctly recognized in both tools; a negation 3+ words away (or outside the ~40-char lookback) is not recognized at all and the clause is silently re-scored as a bare positive claim -- safe when the underlying site is genuinely false (still correctly flagged, just for the 'wrong' textual reason), but a hidden-defect-pass when the underlying site is genuinely true and the clause is a real denial (T2-03). 'Not without' and 'never lacking' (double negation asserting presence) both behave correctly in both tools, confirmed against both a true and a false site.
answers.q3: Partially. The 160-character window correctly rejects a disclosure that is genuinely far away in a long field (tested at 200 chars: correctly flagged as undisclosed) and correctly accepts one written well after a long quote when it is within the window (tested at 120 chars: correctly passes) -- so T1-04's own literal complaint (field-wide search) is fixed. But an undisclosed Qere CAN still pass by standing near another quote's disclosure keyword whenever the two quotes are close enough (roughly within 320 characters of each other) for their two 160-char windows to overlap on the one keyword: I reproduced exactly this with two different verses' real Qere text (MT 1:8, disclosed; MT 3:15, not) 40 characters apart -- both pass silently -- and confirmed the mechanism by widening the gap to 250 characters, which correctly restores the flag on the undisclosed quote alone (T2-04).
answers.q4: The docstrings are honest about MECHANISM and do not over-claim: citation_sweep.py's and check_marks.py's module docstrings both state plainly that a puncta claim 'binds to the verse number written nearest it' and that negation is recognized only when 'adjacent' -- both statements are exactly what the code does, verified by direct execution, including at the edges where that mechanism fails (T2-01/T2-02/T2-03). The gap is one of disclosed LIMITATION, not accuracy: nowhere do the docstrings, TOOLKIT.md, or the code comments warn that 'nearest' is a purely textual/positional notion that a second, unrelated number or a non-adjacent negation can exploit in either direction. normalize_hebrew_in_json.py's new paragraph explaining the book-wide Qere design is accurate and its central compensating-control claim (citation_sweep.py enforces per-verse binding) is independently confirmed true by my own wrong-verse test, not just asserted.
answers.q5: No NEW undocumented divergence from the Jer sources was found. The puncta arm, the Qere tier in the Hebrew-quote-binding arm, and the editorial-note K/Q tier are each explicitly and accurately documented as new-for-Ezek in citation_sweep.py's module docstring, check_marks.py's module docstring, and TOOLKIT.md's 'Where Ezekiel's tools differ from Jeremiah's' section -- confirmed by reading the corresponding Jer sources directly: Jer's citation_sweep.py, check_marks.py and normalize_hebrew_in_json.py contain none of these arms at all (no PUNCTA_*, no QERE-tier branch in the Hebrew-walk loop, no KQ dict/build_index Qere logic), so there is nothing un-diffed against Jer, only genuinely new functionality. The only place a Jer-vs-Ezek difference exists in a SHARED arm (kq_web_quote_warn, the WEB-quote WARN arm) is textually identical to Jer's version (book-name substitution only) in both files. My new findings (T2-01..T2-04) are residual weaknesses WITHIN the new-for-Ezek arms themselves, not parity gaps against Jer.
